newsitem.title: CANADA: Ottawa to act as salmon talks with U.S. collapse.
newsitem.headline: Ottawa to act as salmon talks with U.S. collapse.

text.p: Canada announced on Wednesday the breakdown in Pacific salmon negotiations with the United States and said it would enforce restrictions against U.S. fishing vessels travelling through its waters.

A government statement said Fisheries Department staff had been instructed to enforce existing regulations requiring foreign vessels to contact Canadian authorities as they pass through Canadian waters -- or face possible arrest.
"We are deeply disappointed that the United States came to these meetings lacking the authority to negotiate," Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said in a statement.
"Canada will resume negotiations as soon as the United States is prepared to negotiate in good faith. I will be pressing the U.S. government to ensure that its negotiator has a full mandate."

In Vancouver, salmon industry officials feared the collapse of negotiations might lead to chaos on the waters and further endanger dwindling stocks. Pressure to reach a deal was mounting before the salmon run begins in July.
"I don't know what to expect. Relations between the two countries on the fish issue can only continue to deteriorate," said John Sutcliffe of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union.

"We are extremely disappointed. I frankly can't fathom how we can rationally conduct a fishery this summer without an agreement from the United States. Fish wars aren't acceptable when the health of the salmon resource is at stake."
Canada and the United States have been squabbling for years over how to divide the salmon catch in the Pacific Northwest and several attempts to negotiate a settlement have failed.
The statement said the talks in Seattle broke off on Wednesday when U.S. negotiator Mary Beth West "indicated she did not have the authority to make compromises on Fraser River sockeye."
She and Canadian negotiator Yves Fortier resumed negotiations on Tuesday after talks among stakeholders ended inconclusively on May 9, it said.
Canadian representatives said a compromise had appeared within reach this year.

They said the U.S. side had rejected a Canadian proposal to lower Canada's take of coho salmon on the west coast of Vancouver Island -- a key U.S. goal -- in return for a lower U.S. catch of Fraser River salmon.

The statement pointed out that during his meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington on April 8, Prime Minister Jean Chretien had emphasized the urgency of resolving the Pacific salmon dispute.
The measures announced on Wednesday fell short of those of 1994, when Canada imposed stiff fees on U.S. vessels heading for the Alaskan fishery from their base in Seattle.

Depending on the circumstances vessels that violate the requirements to contact Canadian authorities "can be inspected, required to go to a Canadian port or face arrest," the statement said. "U.S. vessels going to and from the Alaskan fishery are subject to these regulations."
Canada's ruling Liberals, in the middle of an election campaign, are locked in a particularly tight battle in British Columbia, where feelings on fish issues run high.
